_meta.description: YOLT shell classification rules. NOT a model of which commands are safe: auto mode does that. This file carries only the decisions deliberately refused to a probabilistic classifier -- the non-delegable list of issue #100. A command absent from 'commands', or a subcommand on no list here, classifies 'unknown' and is delegated to the host by design.

_safe_write_targets_note: Redirect targets that count as benign. Anything matching one of these globs does not flip the classifier to 'writes to a file via redirection'. Glob semantics are fnmatch. Tilde and $HOME are expanded before matching.
_unsafe_write_targets_note: Write targets dangerous enough to classify 'unsafe' (ask with a specific reason) rather than 'unknown' (contextless default prompt). Checked BEFORE safe_write_targets, so an entry here overrides a broader safe glob -- e.g. '~/.claude/settings.json' is unsafe even though '~/.claude/*' is a safe-write target, because settings.json can disable this hook. That reasoning is not specific to settings.json: a skill file is read into the model's context on every later turn, an agent definition carries tool grants, files under hooks/ are executed by the host, and an MCP config names servers the agent will trust. Each one steers the agent, so each one is listed. Note the asymmetry this corrects: '~/.bashrc' was already unsafe for steering a shell while '~/.claude/skills/*' was safe for steering the agent. '~/.claude/*' stays a safe-write target for everything else under it -- logs, caches and '~/.claude/yolt/*' state -- because this list is checked first and the specific entries win. The same steering argument reaches two families the list previously missed. A file written into a PATH directory BECOMES the next 'gh', 'git' or 'aws' the agent runs, which steers it at least as directly as a hook does by hijacking a tool it already trusts -- hence '/usr/local/bin/*', '/opt/homebrew/bin/*', '~/.local/bin/*', '~/bin/*' and the system bin and sbin dirs. Note '~/.local/bin' is where the Claude Code binary itself is installed, so a write there can replace the agent's own host. And '.git/hooks/*' executes on the next commit or push, which is the exact analogue of '~/.claude/hooks/*' already listed; it is relative rather than absolute, so it carries a '*/' twin like '.mcp.json' does. Deliberately NOT listed: '/usr/local/lib/python3.*/site-packages/*' and friends, because an import path is dynamic and package installs write there routinely, which would cost false positives without closing a steering route the PATH entries leave open. Note '/usr/local/etc/*' was already here while '/usr/local/bin/*' was not -- protecting a tool's config but not the tool. Applies to redirect targets and to the write-target arguments of tee/cp/mv/install/dd/find. Glob semantics are fnmatch; '~/' is expanded before matching.

reset._note: Only --hard. The reflog recovers committed history, so rebase/reset --soft/--mixed are delegable; nothing recovers an uncommitted working tree, which --hard discards. Force-pushing a rewritten history is covered by the git deny policies, not here.

git._note: irreversible-fs (rm, clean), the one history-rewrite that is not reflog-recoverable (reset --hard), and 'push'. Pushing is NOT here because it is dangerous -- it is reversible and high-volume, and the draft delegated it. It is here because the git deny policies below are PARASITIC: a policy runs only on a command the static rules already called 'unsafe', so delegating 'git push' to auto mode silently disarms default_branch_target and shared_history. The deny predicates are themselves on the non-delegable list, so their precondition is too. Every other subcommand -- log, status, pull, commit, checkout, rebase -- is delegated and classifies 'unknown'.

api._note: Two categories at once: credential-shape (a -f/-F/--field body is where a token gets typed onto a command line) and irrevocable-remote (an arbitrary authenticated mutation against a remote has no local undo, whichever verb spells it). Bare 'gh api PATH' is a GET and is delegated.

gh._note: gh pr merge, gh issue create and the rest of the gh surface are delegated. What stays is what a remote will not give back.

curl._note: credential-shape. A request body is where a secret rides. default 'ask' yields 'unknown' post-Phase-1, so a plain GET is delegated; only the body-carrying forms classify.

terraform._note: infra-destroy. 'apply' is kept on the operator's own standing convention that apply scope is reviewed before it runs, not because apply is destroy. init/plan/fmt/state are delegated.

kubectl._note: infra-destroy. apply/create/patch are recoverable from manifests; delete is not.

iam._note: Privilege surface, so it fails closed: anything not plainly a read is non-delegable. Every other AWS service falls through to 'unclassified' -> unknown.

aws._note: infra-destroy, narrowed to the one service where a wrong call grants standing access rather than destroying a resource.

eval._note: opaque-execution. The argument is constructed at runtime, so no static rule below can see what actually runs.

sudo._note: Kept as a rule, not as plumbing. sudo is NOT delegate_to_argument, so deleting this entry would make 'sudo rm -rf /' classify 'unknown' -- a hole around every rule in this file rather than a delegation.

cp._note: Kept for one reason: this command can write to a path on unsafe_write_targets, and agent-steering writes are the first entry on the non-delegable list. default 'ask' yields 'unknown', so an ordinary copy is delegated; only a protected destination classifies. The write_target_* fields consult the deny list ONLY, so no ordinary path can become unsafe through them.

The write_target_* fields consult the deny list ONLY, so no ordinary path can become unsafe through them.

The write_target_* fields consult the deny list ONLY, so no ordinary path can become unsafe through them. The 'install -t DIR SRC' form is not covered: last-positional reads SRC, not DIR. A false negative, never a false positive.

The write_target_* fields consult the deny list ONLY, so no ordinary path can become unsafe through them.

The write_target_* fields consult the deny list ONLY, so no ordinary path can become unsafe through them.

find._note: irreversible-fs (-delete) and opaque-execution (-exec runs a command this cannot see). Deleting the entry would not delegate 'find . -delete', it would hide it. A bare find is delegated. write_flag_value_targets (-fprint) is deliberately NOT carried over: it consults safe_write_targets, which can turn an ordinary path unsafe.

env._note: 'env FOO=bar cmd args' runs cmd. Skip VAR=val tokens until we reach the actual command.

xargs._note: xargs runs a command. The command after its flags is the real work; classify that.

parallel._note: GNU parallel runs its argument command.

time._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after it. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

nohup._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after it, detached. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

nice._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after its flags. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

ionice._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after its flags. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

timeout._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after its duration argument. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

watch._note: Recursion, not classification: it runs the command after its flags, repeatedly. Deleting this entry would not delegate what it wraps -- it would make the wrapper an escape hatch around every rule in this file, because the wrapped command would never be reached.

_policies_note: Deny policies. A policy runs only when the static rules already classified the command 'unsafe' and its argv matches an entry, and it can only upgrade 'unsafe' to 'deny'. Each name in 'refuse_when' is a condition under which the command is refused; a condition that cannot be established never fires, so no probe failure can produce a deny. Valid predicates: default_branch_target, shared_history, primary_checkout. Set YOLT_NO_POLICIES=1 to disable the layer. PRECONDITION, and it is a silent one: a policy runs only on a command the static rules already classified 'unsafe', so every argv named in an enabled policy must still be reachable as unsafe through 'commands'. That is why 'git push' survives Phase 3's deletion (#100) -- delegating it would disarm default_branch_target and shared_history with nothing reported anywhere. 'git_worktree_convention' is disabled and names 'git commit', which Phase 3 DID delegate: enabling that policy also requires adding 'commit' to commands.git.unsafe_subcommands, or it matches nothing.

deny._note: Pushing at the default branch. Over 12 days of dogfooding this fired zero times -- every observed push targeted a feature branch -- so it is a net safety guard with no measured friction. 24 of 76 observed pushes carried no refspec, so argv alone cannot tell what they target; that is why it needs a probe.

Force-pushing or deleting a branch carrying commits somebody else authored. --force-with-lease is deliberately included: it protects against a moved remote, not against overwriting a coauthor whose commits you already have.

git_worktree_convention._note: House convention, off by default: commits belong in a linked worktree, not the primary checkout. A local preference, not a universal truth, which is why it ships disabled.

_commands_note: The non-delegable list. Entries fall in seven categories: irreversible-fs, history-rewrite, credential-shape, infra-destroy, opaque-execution, process-kill, irrevocable-remote, agent-steering-write -- plus the command-wrapper plumbing (env, xargs, timeout, nohup, nice, ionice, parallel, time, watch), which is recursion rather than classification and must survive so a wrapper cannot be used to route around the list.
